headline: Chikatetsu is a clipping of 地下鉄道 (chika tetsudō, “underground railway”).
Kippu is 切る (kiru, “cut”) plus 符 (fu, “tally split in half used for identification”).
Daigakusei is 大学 (daigaku, “university”) plus 生 (-sei, “student; pupil”).
Kanji is a Middle Chinese compound, literally “Han Chinese + character”.
Kinō went kinopu → kinoɸu → kinowu → kinou → kinoː, and its initial ki is unclear.
Mon is from Middle Chinese 門 (MC mwon).
Atsui for weather and 熱い for objects share one source: Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *atu.
Ireru developed from the classical lower bigrade verb 入る, meaning to put something into something.
Yureru comes from the lower bigrade intransitive classical verb 揺る (yuru).
Iku has a hidden twin: yuku, thanks to an old habit of inserting a y glide before vowels.
Shinsetsu is literally “blood relative + close”, a Middle Chinese compound.
Ushiro may be from us- (“lost; gone”) plus a locative suffix, but the ultimate derivation is unknown.
Tonari may be 外 (to1, “outside, other”) plus nari, but the source gives two analyses of the second part.
Maitsuki is “every + month” and is first attested in roughly 1215.
Isogashii is derived from the verb 急ぐ (isogu, “to hurry”), first attested in a text from 850.
Hyaku is borrowed from Middle Chinese 百 (MC paek, literally “hundred”).
Hikōki is first attested in 1908, and is 飛行 (hikō, “flying, flight”) plus 機 (-ki, “machine”), a calque of English flying machine.
Boku shifted from the kun'yomi of shimobe or yatsugare to the on'yomi, and became prevalent around the Meiji period.
Hairu is from older 這ひ入る (fafiiru): a compound of 這ひ (fafi, from 這ふ, “to crawl”) plus 入る (iru, “to enter”).
Kanashii historically also meant “dear; beloved; lovely”, in addition to “sad”.
Nuru is possibly related to 濡れる (nureru, “to get wet”).
Higashi was hingashi: /ɸiŋɡaɕi/ → /ɸiɡaɕi/ → /hiɡaɕi/.
Wataru is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *wataru.
Hachi is from Middle Chinese 八 (MC peat).
Kuroi is Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Kyaku is from Middle Chinese 客 (MC khaek).
Betsu is from Ainu ペッ (pet, “water, river”), and its kanji spelling is an example of ateji.
Ongaku is from Middle Chinese 音樂.
